Chapter 3: The Trap of Drifting and the Power of Purpose.
There’s a certain comfort in routine, isn’t there? Waking up at the same time every day, following the same route to work, spending weekends in all the familiar ways. For a lot of us, that predictability feels safe—almost like a cozy blanket.
But if you look a little deeper, something else might be happening. There’s this slow drift away from living with intention. It’s like quietly surrendering to the status quo, day by day.
The thing is, drifting isn’t always obvious. Sometimes, it even looks like success—a steady job, a nice home, a calendar full of plans. But inside, maybe you feel a bit restless, like life is just happening to someone else. Days blur into weeks, and weeks into years. And those dreams that once felt so urgent? They start to fade into the background.
Think about a teacher who once felt passionate about inspiring her students. Now, she finds herself just going through the motions. The lessons are the same, the faces change, but the spark is gone. She tells herself she’s just tired, but deep down, she knows she’s lost sight of why she started teaching in the first place. The routine has turned into a cage, and she’s not quite sure how to break free.
That’s the real trap of drifting: living by default, not by design. It creeps in when we make choices out of habit, when we care more about what others think than what we truly want, when we choose comfort over growth. Most people don’t even notice it until one day, they wake up and wonder—where did all the time go?
Now, here’s something to pay attention to: the antidote to drifting is purpose. Not just any purpose, but a clear, specific sense of direction—a reason to get up in the morning, a goal that genuinely feels worth chasing. Purpose acts like a compass, cutting through the fog of routine and pointing you forward.
But let’s be honest—finding your purpose isn’t always easy. It means asking yourself some tough questions. Things like, “What do I actually care about? What am I willing to struggle for? What would I keep doing, even if nobody else approved?” There aren’t quick answers here. It takes honesty, a bit of soul-searching, and sometimes, the courage to disappoint others.
Picture a man who spent years climbing the corporate ladder. He finally reaches the top, only to realize he’s been chasing someone else’s dream all along. Sure, the money and status are nice, but they don’t fill that emptiness inside. It’s only when he takes a sabbatical—stepping away from all the noise and expectations—that he starts to rediscover what really matters to him. He begins volunteering, mentoring young people, and eventually, he changes careers entirely. It’s not an easy shift, but for the first time in years, he feels truly alive.
The thing is, purpose doesn’t have to be grand or world-changing. Sometimes, it’s as simple as wanting to be a good parent, to create something beautiful, or to help others in small ways. The most important part? That it’s chosen by you—not inherited, and not forced upon you.
When you have purpose, you get this new energy. Decisions suddenly feel easier. Setbacks aren’t as overwhelming. And that old temptation to drift? It starts to fade away. Life takes on a new kind of meaning, and even the hard days feel worthwhile. The journey might not always be smooth, but now, it’s guided by something deeper than habit—or fear.
